summary.text: For a prime \(p\), the only admissible integers up to \(p\) are \(1\) and \(p\), so \(a(p)=2\). Taking \(\epsilon=1/2\) and an arbitrarily large prime \(p\ge e^5\) would force \(\sqrt{\log p}\le2\), hence \(\log p\le4\), contradicting \(\log p\ge5\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=\#\{k\in\mathbb N:1\le k\le n\text{ and every prime factor of }k\text{ divides }n\}.
\]
We disprove the assertion that, for every \(\epsilon>0\), one has
\[
a(n)\ge (\log n)^{1-\epsilon}
\]
for every sufficiently large \(n\).

The key observation is that \(a(p)=2\) for every prime number \(p\). Indeed, the set of prime factors of a prime \(p\) is the singleton \(\{p\}\). Certainly \(1\) is counted by \(a(p)\), because \(1\) has no prime factors, and \(p\) itself is counted. Conversely, suppose that \(1\le k\le p\) and every prime factor of \(k\) belongs to \(\{p\}\). If \(k=1\), this is one of the two integers already listed. If \(k>1\), then \(k\) has a prime divisor \(q\). By the assumed containment of prime-factor sets, \(q=p\), so \(p\mid k\). Since \(k>0\), divisibility gives \(p\le k\), while by hypothesis \(k\le p\). Thus \(k=p\). Hence the only counted integers are \(1\) and \(p\), proving
\[
a(p)=2. \tag{1}
\]

Now suppose, for contradiction, that the conjectured statement were true. Apply it with
\[
\epsilon=\frac12>0.
\]
There would then be a natural number \(N\) such that for every natural number \(n\ge N\),
\[
(\log n)^{1/2}\le a(n). \tag{2}
\]

Choose a natural number
\[
M=\lceil e^5\rceil.
\]
There is a prime \(p\) with
\[
p\ge \max\{N,M\}.
\]
Here we use the standard fact that primes are unbounded. For completeness, this follows from Euclid's argument: given any bound, form one plus the factorial of a sufficiently large integer exceeding that bound; any prime divisor of the resulting number cannot divide the factorial and therefore must exceed the chosen integer. Thus a prime can always be found beyond any prescribed finite bound.

Since \(p\ge N\), inequality (2), together with (1), gives
\[
(\log p)^{1/2}\le a(p)=2. \tag{3}
\]
Because \(p\ge2\), we have \(\log p\ge0\). We may therefore square (3), preserving the inequality. Equivalently, using the usual identity \(((\log p)^{1/2})^2=\log p\) for a nonnegative real number, we obtain
\[
\log p\le 4. \tag{4}
\]

On the other hand, the choice of \(M\) and \(p\) gives
\[
e^5\le \lceil e^5\rceil=M\le p.
\]
The logarithm is increasing on the positive real numbers, so
\[
5=\log(e^5)\le \log p. \tag{5}
\]
Combining (4) and (5) yields
\[
5\le \log p\le4,
\]
which is impossible.

Therefore the proposed eventual lower bound fails already for \(\epsilon=\tfrac12\). In fact, the underlying reason is stronger: along the unbounded sequence of prime arguments, \(a(p)\) is constantly equal to \(2\), whereas \((\log p)^{1/2}\) tends to infinity. Hence it is false that for every \(\epsilon>0\), \(a(n)\ge(\log n)^{1-\epsilon}\) for all sufficiently large \(n\).
